reasoning_summary:
Step-by-step verification, in order.

0001 (construction): Aut(Heawood) = PGL(2,7), order 336, with the index-2 subgroup preserving each side of the bipartition being PSL(2,7) (= PGL(3,2), the Fano collineation group). Adding a clique on the 7 point-vertices raises their degree from 3 to 9 while line-vertices stay at degree 3, so every automorphism preserves the two sides; restricted to the cross edges it is a side-preserving Heawood automorphism. Hence Aut = PSL(2,7) on 14 vertices. Justified.

0007-0013 (Fano restatement): the point/line incidence graph is exactly the Heawood graph, plus a clique on point-vertices; the remark that the clique kills the point-line duality is the same degree argument. Justified.

0017 (lower bound 7 and 7-vertex check): Aut(G) <= S_n forces n >= 7 since PSL(2,7) has minimal faithful permutation degree 7. 1044 is the correct count of graphs on 7 vertices, and the claim is independently true: any faithful degree-7 action of PSL(2,7) is the Fano point (or line) action, which is 2-transitive, so the only invariant graphs are K_7 and its complement, with Aut = S_7. Justified.

0019: PSL(2,7) has 8 Sylow 7-subgroups, hence 48 elements of order 7, so sigma exists and tau outside <sigma> exists. With 8 <= n <= 13, an order-7 automorphism has orbits of size 1 or 7, at least one (it is not the identity) and at most one (no room for two). Justified.

0021: n <= 13 with |A| = |B| = 7 forces A ∩ B nonempty, so <sigma, tau> is transitive on A ∪ B; any v outside A ∪ B is fixed by both generators, hence by the whole group, so its adjacency to A ∪ B is constant. That uniformity is exactly what makes every automorphism of H = G[A ∪ B] extend to G by fixing outside vertices pointwise. Justified.

0025 (Case 1, A = B): sigma|_A and tau|_A are 7-cycles generating a transitive subgroup of Sym(A). Among transitive subgroups of S_7 (C_7, D_7, F_21, F_42, PSL(2,7), A_7, S_7), the ones with a normal Sylow 7 (D_7, F_21, F_42) cannot be generated by two 7-cycles, leaving C_7, PSL(2,7), A_7. The write-up says 'S_7' where 'A_7' is correct (7-cycles are even, so S_7 is unreachable), but this is a labeling slip that does not affect the argument: the third alternative is discarded solely because its order (2520 for A_7, 5040 for S_7) exceeds 168, and C_7 is excluded because tau is not a power of sigma. So <sigma, tau> is PSL(2,7) and, having order 168 = |Aut(G)|, equals Aut(G).

0027: since Aut(G) = <sigma, tau> fixes every vertex outside A pointwise and preserves A, restriction Aut(G) -> Aut(G[A]) is injective, and by 0021 it is surjective. So G[A] is a 7-vertex graph with automorphism group PSL(2,7), contradicting 0017. Justified.

0031 (Case 2, A != B): A\B and B\A are nonempty; complementation preserves Aut, A and B, so assuming vw is an edge is legitimate. tau fixes v and is transitive on B, giving v adjacent to all of B. sigma fixes w (w not in A) and is transitive on A, so every vertex of A is adjacent to w; reapplying tau to each v' in A\B (which tau fixes) gives all edges between A\B and B. Justified.

0033: 'A ∪ B' here is a typo for 'A ∩ B' (nonempty by n <= 13); the previous step gives complete bipartite adjacency between S = A\B and T = A ∩ B inside A. Identifying A with Z_7 via sigma, the edge set is a union of difference classes; for every d != 0 there is x in S with x + d in T, since otherwise S + d = S would force S = Z_7 or S empty. So all six differences occur and A is a clique; the symmetric argument (all edges between B\A and A, then B\A vs A ∩ B) makes B a clique, and together with the A\B to B\A edges, A ∪ B is complete. Justified.

0035: |A ∪ B| = 14 - |A ∩ B| >= 8, so G[A ∪ B] complete on at least 8 vertices contributes at least 8! = 40320 automorphisms, each extending to G by 0021, contradicting |Aut(G)| = 168. Justified.

The two cases are exhaustive for the chosen tau, covering all n in 8..13, so 14 is minimal. Only defects found are cosmetic: 'S_7' for 'A_7' in step 0025 (both dismissed by the identical order argument) and 'A ∪ B' for 'A ∩ B' in step 0033. Neither breaks the chain of reasoning.
